title: Controlling a stage: purpose, objectives and context
blurb: Explain why the project manager runs controlling a stage, what it must achieve and where it sits between the board, the teams and the other processes.
question: During a delivery stage, a project manager assigns work to teams, reviews their progress and fixes a small slippage without involving the board. Which process is being used, and what is its purpose?

teach.body: Formally: controlling a stage exists to assign work, monitor that work, handle issues, report progress to the project board and take corrective action, so the stage stays within the tolerances the board has set. In plain English: once the board authorizes a stage, this is how the project manager runs it day to day, keeping it on track and only going back to the board when the stage tolerances are under threat.

teach.caption: The project manager repeats this loop throughout every delivery stage. The tolerances it protects are stage tolerances, set by the project board.

teach.h: Objectives: controlling a stage makes sure that...
items: Attention stays on delivering the stage's products, and any drift from the products and delivery method agreed at the start of the stage is watched so change does not go uncontrolled.
Risks and issues are kept under control.
The business case is kept under review.
The agreed products for the stage meet the agreed quality expectations and are accepted.
The project management team focuses on delivery within the tolerances that have been set.

items.label: Starting up a project (no stage yet)
Initiating a project, then a stage boundary
Controlling a stage + managing product delivery, then a stage boundary
Controlling a stage + managing product delivery + closing a project

teach.caption: Directing a project runs above all of this from the end of starting up to closure.

teach.h: What happens as a stage nears its end
Who controlling a stage talks to
head: Link
What flows
rows: Stage or exception plan authorized in; highlight reports, exception reports and requests for advice out; board advice back
Work packages authorized out; checkpoint reports, new issues or risks and completed work package notices back
Triggered when a stage boundary approaches
Triggered when the project end approaches

teach.h: Controlling a stage vs managing a stage boundary

rows.label: When
values: At or near the end of a stage

rows.label: Plans
values: Work packages; stage plan kept up to date
Next stage plan or exception plan

teach.h: Worked scenario: a water meter rollout
teach.body: At Fenwick Water, project manager Priya Nair is running stage 2 of a smart meter project. She authorizes work packages for two installation teams, reads their checkpoint reports and sends executive Graham Lowe's board a fortnightly highlight report. When one team falls three days behind, she moves a fitter across from the other team: the stage stays within tolerance, so that is corrective action and the board simply sees it in the next highlight report.

teach.text: Classic traps: (1) Reporting highlights at an agreed frequency belongs to controlling a stage, NOT managing a stage boundary. (2) If the problem can be fixed within stage tolerance, the PM takes corrective action; no exception report is needed. (3) Exception plans are prepared in managing a stage boundary, not here. (4) The business case is kept under review during the stage too, not only at its end.

items: Purpose: assign work, monitor it, handle issues, report to the board and take corrective action within stage tolerances.
Run by the project manager at the managing level.
Starts when the board authorizes a stage or an exception plan.
Hands over to managing a stage boundary, or in the final stage to closing a project.
Objectives include keeping the business case under review and getting the stage's products accepted.

summary: You can now state the purpose and objectives of controlling a stage and explain how it links the board, the teams and the stage boundary and closing processes. You can also tell it apart from managing a stage boundary.

A.q: Which is a purpose of the controlling a stage process?
options: Give the board what it needs to review the current stage
Control the link between project manager and team manager
Assign work, monitor it and keep the stage within tolerance
Provide a fixed point to confirm the project product is accepted
A.why: Controlling a stage assigns and monitors work, handles issues, reports to the board and takes corrective action so the stage stays within the board's tolerances (manual 16.1).

whyNot.0: Giving the board what it needs to review the stage is the purpose of managing a stage boundary.
whyNot.1: Controlling the link between project manager and team manager is the purpose of managing product delivery.
whyNot.3: A fixed point for confirming acceptance is the purpose of closing a project.

A.q:
Identify the missing word in the following sentence.
In controlling a stage, the project manager takes [?] action so that the stage remains within the tolerances set by the project board.
options: exception
corrective
escalation
assurance
A.why: The purpose of controlling a stage includes taking corrective action to keep the stage within tolerance (manual 16.1).

whyNot.0: Exception relates to a forecast breach of tolerance, which is escalated rather than corrected by the PM.
whyNot.2: Escalation goes to the board when tolerance is forecast to be exceeded; it does not keep the stage within tolerance.
whyNot.3: Assurance is the board's responsibility and is not an action the PM takes to stay within tolerance.

A.q: Which role carries out the controlling a stage process?
options: The project board, at the directing level
Team managers, at the delivering level
The business layer, outside the project
The project manager, at the managing level
A.why: Controlling a stage is one of the managing-level processes run by the project manager.

whyNot.0: The board uses directing a project and does not manage the stage day to day.
whyNot.1: Team managers use managing product delivery.
whyNot.2: The business layer sets project tolerances and commissions the project; it does not run stages.

B.q:
Which two statements are objectives of the controlling a stage process?
1. The business case is kept under review.
2. Open issues and risks have follow-on action recommendations.
3. The project management team focuses on delivery within the established tolerances.
4. Any benefits already realized are assessed.
options: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
B.why: Keeping the business case under review (1) and focusing the team on delivery within tolerances (3) are objectives of controlling a stage (manual 16.2).

whyNot.0: Statement 2 is an objective of closing a project.
whyNot.2: Statements 2 and 4 are both objectives of closing a project.
whyNot.3: Statement 4 is an objective of closing a project.

B.q: Why does controlling a stage monitor any movement away from the products and delivery method agreed at the start of the stage?
options: To avoid uncontrolled change
To prepare the end stage report
To set work package tolerances
To trigger a premature closure
B.why: One objective of controlling a stage is that drift from the agreed products and delivery method is monitored so that change does not go uncontrolled (manual 16.2).

whyNot.1: The end stage report is prepared in managing a stage boundary, not as the reason for this monitoring.
whyNot.2: The PM sets work package tolerances when authorizing work packages, not as the aim of this monitoring.
whyNot.3: Premature closure is triggered by the project board, not by stage monitoring.

B.q: A supplier delivery is late, but the project manager forecasts that the stage will still finish within its time and cost tolerances. What should the PM do?
options: Raise an exception report to the board
Prepare an exception plan for approval
Ask the board to authorize a new stage
Take corrective action within the stage
B.why: Within stage tolerance the PM handles the problem in controlling a stage by taking corrective action; only a forecast breach of stage tolerance is escalated (manual 16.1, 11.2.6).

whyNot.0: An exception report is needed when stage tolerance is forecast to be exceeded, which is not the case here.
whyNot.1: Exception plans follow a board request after an exception report.
whyNot.2: A new stage is authorized at a stage boundary, not to absorb a delay within tolerance.

C.q: In which process are highlight reports produced, and who receives them?
options: Controlling a stage; the project board
Managing a stage boundary; the project board
Managing product delivery; the project manager
Directing a project; the business layer
C.why: The PM produces highlight reports in controlling a stage (report highlights) for the project board at the agreed frequency.

whyNot.1: Managing a stage boundary produces the end stage report, not regular highlight reports.
whyNot.2: Team managers in managing product delivery send checkpoint reports to the PM.
whyNot.3: Directing a project is the board's process; it receives highlight reports rather than producing them.

C.q: What starts the controlling a stage process, and what brings it to an end?
options: A project mandate arrives; the PID is approved
A work package is accepted; completion is notified
A stage is authorized; a stage or project end nears
An end stage report is approved; closure is notified
C.why: Controlling a stage starts when the board authorizes a stage (or an exception plan) and hands over when a stage boundary or the project end approaches.

whyNot.0: A mandate triggers starting up a project, and PID approval ends initiation.
whyNot.1: Accepting a work package and notifying completion are managing product delivery activities.
whyNot.3: The end stage report supports the board's next-stage decision, and closure notification ends the project.

C.q: How do controlling a stage and managing product delivery differ in viewpoint?
options: CS is the board's view; MP is the PM's view
CS is the PM's view; MP is the board's view
CS is the team's view; MP is the PM's view
CS is the PM's view; MP is the team's view
C.why: Controlling a stage is the project manager's view of the work; managing product delivery is the team manager's view. The board is not involved in managing product delivery.

whyNot.0: The board works through directing a project, not controlling a stage.
whyNot.1: The board is not involved in managing product delivery.
whyNot.2: Team managers work in managing product delivery, not controlling a stage.

reteach.title: The head chef during service
reteach.question: A restaurant owner agrees the evening's budget and timings, then leaves the head chef to run the kitchen. What does the chef do all evening?

blocks.body: The chef assigns dishes to each station, watches progress, deals with problems, tells the owner how the night is going and moves people around when one station falls behind. Only if the night will blow the agreed limits does the chef call the owner for a decision. That is controlling a stage: the PM runs the stage within the board's tolerances and escalates only a forecast breach.

blocks.text: The chef does not phone the owner for every burnt pan. Within tolerance, the PM acts; beyond tolerance, the PM escalates.

explain.body: Controlling a stage keeps the stage within the tolerances set by the project board. The business layer sets project tolerances; the PM sets work package tolerances.

test.q: Who sets the tolerances that controlling a stage aims to stay within?
options: The project board
The business layer
The project manager
The team manager
test.why: Controlling a stage keeps the stage within the stage tolerances set by the project board (manual 16.1).

whyNot.1: The business layer sets project tolerances, not stage tolerances.
whyNot.2: The PM sets work package tolerances for team managers.
whyNot.3: Team managers work within work package tolerances set by the PM.

explain.body: Focus on the stage's products, control risks and issues, keep the business case under review, get products accepted to quality expectations, and keep the team delivering within tolerance.

test.q: Which is an objective of the controlling a stage process?
options: There is authority to close the project
The stage's agreed products are accepted
The business can support the products later
A stage plan is prepared for the next stage
test.why: Controlling a stage ensures the agreed products for the stage meet quality expectations and are accepted (manual 16.2).

whyNot.0: Authority to close is an objective of directing a project.
whyNot.2: Making sure the business can support products after closure is an objective of closing a project.
whyNot.3: Preparing the next stage plan is an objective of managing a stage boundary.

explain.body: In delivery stages, controlling a stage hands over to managing a stage boundary. In the final stage there is no boundary: closing a project runs inside that stage instead.

test.q: In the final stage, which process does controlling a stage hand over to as the project end approaches?
options: Managing a stage boundary
Directing a project
Closing a project
Initiating a project
test.why: In the final stage, controlling a stage triggers closing a project when the project end approaches; a stage boundary is not run at the end of the final stage.

whyNot.0: Managing a stage boundary is not used at the end of the final stage.
whyNot.1: Directing a project runs throughout and authorizes closure, but it is closing a project that is triggered here.
whyNot.3: Initiating a project happens once, in the initiation stage.

explain.body: The board manages by exception. Between stage ends it is kept informed by the PM's highlight reports at the agreed frequency, and by exception reports if tolerance is threatened.

test.q: How is the project board kept informed of stage progress without managing day to day?
options: Through checkpoint reports from the teams
Through reading the PM's daily log
Through the end project report each month
Through highlight reports from the PM
test.why: The PM produces highlight reports for the board at the agreed frequency in controlling a stage.

whyNot.0: Checkpoint reports go from team managers to the PM, not to the board.
whyNot.1: The daily log is the PM's informal diary, not a board reporting tool.
whyNot.2: The end project report is produced once, in closing a project.
